name: Lateral Ankle Sprain
summary: Injury of the lateral ankle ligament complex, most commonly the ATFL, often after inversion with plantar flexion.

looksLike: Feeling of giving way in more severe or recurrent injury
redFlags: Ottawa Ankle Rules indication for radiography
Severe syndesmotic tenderness or inability to progress weight bearing
Persistent pain suggesting osteochondral or tendon injury
firstSteps: External support with brace or taping based on severity

assess: Ottawa ankle/foot rule screening where relevant
Balance and hopping capacity during later rehab

tests.name: Anterior Drawer Test — Ankle
tests.purpose: Assess anterior talar translation, primarily stressing the ATFL.
tests.positive: Excess anterior translation, soft/absent endpoint, apprehension or concordant lateral ankle pain.

tests.name: Talar Tilt — Inversion
tests.purpose: Assess lateral ligament integrity with emphasis on CFL.
tests.positive: Excess inversion tilt or pain with a soft endpoint.

stages.label: Protection & Optimal Loading
stages.goal: Protect tissue, control swelling and restore safe gait.
do: External support with brace or taping based on severity
Short immobilization only for severe injury when clinically indicated
dose: Ankle pumps/circles: 10–20 reps, 3–5 times/day within comfortable range
Isometric eversion/plantar flexion/dorsiflexion: 3–5 sets of 20–30 s at tolerable effort
Gait practice frequently in short bouts
moveOn: Swelling and resting pain trending down

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Balance
stages.goal: Restore dorsiflexion, ankle strength and sensorimotor control.
when: Swelling and resting pain trending down
dose: Calf raises: 3 x 8–15, progress double to single leg
Single-leg balance: 3 x 30–60 s, progress surface/vision/reach
moveOn: Able to perform repeated heel raises and stairs without meaningful instability

stages.label: Running, Landing & Return
stages.goal: Restore dynamic stability and reduce recurrence risk.
when: Able to perform repeated heel raises and stairs without meaningful instability
do: Brace for higher-risk activity when appropriate
dose: Hop/landing drills: 2–4 sets of 5–10 quality reps
moveOn: Full training/work tasks tolerated without reactive swelling

returnCriteria: Repeated heel raises and hops without instability

logic: After excluding fracture and major syndesmotic injury, early protected loading is usually better than unnecessary prolonged immobilization.
Restore dorsiflexion, calf/peroneal strength, balance and later hopping/cutting capacity.
Return to sport should be criteria-based.
structures: Posterior talofibular ligament in severe injury
mechanism: Sudden inversion, often with plantar flexion
classification: Grade I: microscopic stretch with little or no instability
Grade II: partial tear with moderate swelling, pain and functional loss
Grade III: complete tear with marked instability; exclude fracture and associated injury
investigations: Use Ottawa Ankle Rules to guide radiography after acute trauma.
Ultrasound/MRI may be considered when symptoms persist, diagnosis is uncertain or major associated injury is suspected.
manual: Pain-free ankle/foot joint mobilization can be used alongside exercise.
Anterior-to-posterior talar mobilization or weight-bearing MWM may be used when dorsiflexion is restricted.
Soft-tissue techniques may assist short-term pain/swelling but should not replace loading and balance rehabilitation.
Soft-tissue treatment when it improves movement comfort
Talocrural posterior glide/MWM can be used when dorsiflexion is limited.
Retest the weight-bearing lunge immediately after mobilization.
Soft-tissue work can be used after acute bruising/hematoma settles.
modalities: Cryotherapy may be used briefly for symptom relief; it is not the rehabilitation itself.
Compression is useful for swelling management.
Do not use taping/bracing as a stand-alone treatment for chronic ankle instability.
Compression and elevation early if swelling is significant
Cold can be used briefly for comfort
Avoid prolonged immobilization in uncomplicated sprains
Compression/elevation early if swelling is significant.
Cold 10–15 minutes for comfort if useful; it is not required for healing.
dosing: Calf raises: progress double-leg to single-leg, 2–4 sets × 8–20 reps.
Later hopping/landing: low volume first, then multidirectional work.
progression: Walk without limp → single-leg control → hopping → running → cutting
Use functional criteria rather than time alone for return to sport
Achieve good single-leg balance and calf strength before higher-speed tasks.
Progress hopping → running → cutting → sport practice.
mistakes: Prolonged complete rest without a clinical reason
Returning to sport before hopping and change-of-direction tolerance
Treating a single special test as proof of a specific ligament tear
Ignoring syndesmosis, fracture, osteochondral or tendon injury when symptoms or mechanism do not fit a routine lateral sprain
Increasing running and cutting volume together before the ankle tolerates each demand separately
Keeping the ankle immobilized too long.
Returning to sport because swelling is gone while hop control remains poor.
Forcing painful stretching in the first days.
pearls: Inversion + plantar flexion strongly points toward ATFL mechanism.
Recurrent sprain requires assessment of dorsiflexion, balance and proximal kinetic chain, not only the ligament.
Reassess weight-bearing ability, swelling distribution, bony tenderness and neurovascular status; do not assume every inversion injury is a simple sprain.
Use the Ottawa Ankle Rules as a radiography decision aid when applicable, not as a substitute for clinical judgment.
Progress loading by gait quality, symptom response and next-day swelling rather than by a fixed calendar alone.
Return-to-sport decisions should combine confidence with strength, balance, hopping, landing and change-of-direction capacity; pain-free walking alone is insufficient.
education: Encourage safe early movement and loading.
Explain that brace/tape can support return to sport but does not replace balance and strength training.
Teach signs that require reassessment such as inability to progress weight bearing.
escalation: Medical imaging/review when fracture or syndesmotic injury is suspected or recovery is not following an expected course

tests.name: Anterior Drawer Test — Ankle
tests.purpose: Assess anterior talar translation, primarily stressing the ATFL.
tests.positive: Excess anterior translation, soft/absent endpoint, apprehension or concordant lateral ankle pain.
tests.patientPosition: Sitting or supine with the lower leg supported; ankle in slight plantar flexion.
tests.therapistPosition: In front of the tested ankle.
tests.handPlacement: One hand stabilizes the distal tibia; the other cups the posterior calcaneus/talus.
procedure: Gently draw the calcaneus/talus anteriorly while the tibia remains fixed.
Compare translation and end-feel with the opposite ankle.
tests.interpretation: Supports ATFL injury/laxity; interpret with history, palpation and comparison side.

tests.name: Talar Tilt — Inversion
tests.purpose: Assess lateral ligament integrity with emphasis on CFL.
tests.positive: Excess inversion tilt or pain with a soft endpoint.
tests.patientPosition: Sitting or supine with the ankle near neutral.
tests.therapistPosition: At the foot of the patient.
tests.handPlacement: Stabilize distal tibia/fibula with one hand; grasp calcaneus with the other.
procedure: Invert the talus/calcaneus in a controlled manner.
Compare tilt, pain and end-feel with the opposite side.

story.headline: The ankle that rolled—and the detective who checked the bones first
story.scene: Second half. A footballer lands on another player's shoe. His foot tips inward, the outside of the ankle hurts, and within minutes the swelling arrives like an uninvited spectator. He limps into your clinic insisting, 'It's only a sprain. I watched three videos.'
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Can you just tape it so I can play tomorrow?' Therapist: 'First we check whether the bones have voted against that plan.'
story.clue: Inversion, especially with plantar flexion, makes lateral ligament injury plausible. But focal bony tenderness and weight-bearing ability matter before you reach for a ligament stress test.
story.twist: A sprain and a fracture can share the same dramatic entrance. Use the Ottawa Ankle Rules appropriately; neither the amount of swelling nor a single drawer test tells the whole story.
story.aha: Pain improved is not the same as ankle stability restored. Balance, strength and sport-specific landing still need rehearsal.
story.patientTranslation: The supporting bands on the outside of the ankle may have been stretched or torn. We first check for signs of fracture, then help you walk, move, strengthen and regain balance at a safe pace.
story.clinicianReasoning: Screen bony tenderness, neurovascular status, syndesmosis and weight bearing. Assess ATFL/CFL and dorsiflexion when tolerated. Progress rehabilitation by swelling response, force production, balance and functional exposure—not the date on the calendar.
story.rehabBridge: Act one: protect and walk safely. Act two: restore dorsiflexion, calf/peroneal strength and balance. Finale: hops, cutting and confidence without reactive swelling.
story.question: After inversion trauma, there is posterior-edge lateral malleolar bony tenderness. What comes before aggressive ankle stress testing?
options: Consider radiography using Ottawa Ankle Rules
Clear the athlete because they can wiggle their toes
story.explanation: Bony tenderness at the specified malleolar sites meets an Ottawa Ankle Rules imaging criterion; screen for fracture before provocative ligament assessment.
